en: While my lion-hearted uncle lived,
We grew to manhood as lions.
After my uncle Semetey passed away,
We who were white steel became notched,
We who were heroes fell into sorrow,
We were parted from the renowned lion.
Foster-father Kyzylsart,
Our backs made sore, to Kyyaz
We came as docile pacers.
Parted from our good fortune,
In Jeti-Özön, among the Jediger,
To Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
We came as spoils of war.
Our herds were plundered,
Our blood was utterly drained,
Separated from the six divisions,
Our strength departed long ago.
I bear a deep-dug wound,
I bear a vast, seething misery.
Longing to die, I cannot die,
Yet cannot take my own life.
Our herds were given over to plunder,
Barely a spoonful of blood remains.
I am fading away.
Foster-father Kyzylsart,
Please take us as your companions.
The stars in heaven have turned pale,
My father was your old friend.
I am frozen by the cold—give me your coat;
I beg you with both hands outstretched.
My strength is gone—give me your medicine,
O noble, khanly father,
Give me all your remedies.
I beg you, father, grant me your best;
Give me your hand and do not abandon me.”
Thus did Külchoro
Speak in his wretchedness, and then
His foster-father Kyzylsart—
Finding no head he could tear off,
His courage like a sheer mountain ridge,
The formidable Külchoro
Seemed able to devour any man he grappled.
At Choro’s terrible bearing,
All the Jediger might flee.
If seven hosts of alien foes came,
He alone could crush them.
The hot breath from his mouth
Seemed able to set the valley aflame.
If he merely stirred,
He seemed able to ravage the world.
Broad-hearted as a valley,
His handsome front teeth
Were like tempered steel.
When you looked at his aquiline nose,
It was like the sheath of a saber.
His upturned mustache
Was like a Bukharan blade.
The heat of his two eyes
Was like flame rising through a valley.
When you looked into their corners,
They were like the hollows of dried-up wells.
When that formidable man moved,
He seemed able to swallow the world.
Recovering from his broken state,
Choro became a bloodthirsty warrior again.
His former vigor
Filled him like a bloated blue tick,
And his wolfish valor and heroism
Were as they had been before.
The awe-inspiring poor falcon’s
Hollows filled with milk,
His gaunt frame filled with flesh,
And the time came for him to fight.
With Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
The time came for him to meet face-to-face.
His figure was like half a mountain,
Ready to devour any soul he met.
Külchoro, upheld by the divine,
Used Choro as his pretext,
And the poor fellow followed him about.
The blue mastiff left by the hero—
Kyzylsart suddenly seized it
And slaughtered the blue mastiff.
Cutting out its diaphragm,
He laid it upon Külchoro.
Kyzylsart was meticulous,
Skillful in devising strange measures.
Upon Külchoro’s back
He fitted the dog’s diaphragm,
And the powdered red medicine
He rubbed on forty times.
The boiled black medicine
He rubbed on time after time.
Then the poor father Choro’s
Painful places subsided,
His eyes opened wide,
Blood coursed through his body,
And the day came when his courage swelled.
The moon waned and the nights passed,
And many days went by.
Vigor seethed and strength filled him,
Power welled up within him.
The days passed as though he lay in comfort,
And all he saw was like the Night of Glory.
His loosened joints were restored,
And all his sorrow disappeared.
His thoughts became a night of blessed destiny,
And the spirited youth and swift horse
Came to the day their worth was fulfilled.
It was then that Külchoro
Returned to himself and recovered.
Kyzylsart had been his healer,
And all his affliction disappeared.
His courage rose and strength filled him.
Think of Choro now:
He could find no mountain to strike,
No enemy to fight,
No stone to chew.
You girded your appointed belt,
And raised turmoil against all who faced you.
You besieged the Khagan and took his lands,
And conquered the populous Chinese realm
That even the Prophet could not have entered.
You reached it, broke it, and took the land;
O hero, you shattered Jerken and attacked it.
While you were in your prime,
You raided Jet-Kait and took booty.
You routed the myriad host and leveled it.
Kara-Shaar and Kambyl
You besieged, subdued, and opened as a road.
Solon, Shive, and Manchu
You beat like wool and brought low.
You leveled them with your inlaid spear,
And while your lion lived,
You made the people suffer and ruled them.
Your might became known.
One of your names was inscribed
In the records of Beijing.
While your noble prince lived,
You drove white deer and made them cattle.
You stirred turmoil throughout the world,
And made bullets rain from your cartridge pouch.
While your hero lived,
You crushed every foe you faced.
The six keen blades fallen from heaven,
Calling them your paternal inheritance,
You bound them at your slender waist
And subdued the world alone.
You were a lion, but became a wanderer;
You were parted from your valiant one.
You burned and grieved until you became thus.
Parted from the noble hero,
You became a herdsman’s slave.
You were a mountain pass, but became a road;
Parted from the renowned lion,
You fell into abject disgrace.
Today speak your truth without wavering.
Will the divinely favored lion
Stand by without raising battle?
Will God strike Choro down
Before he fights and takes revenge?
The gold-jawed, cast-iron-headed mace—
When you see its venom, flee far away.
Gripping it and swinging it in his hand,
He raised a black stone as large as a house
And hurled it with both hands.
Sparks flew from his mace,
Flames blazed and crackled,
And fire sprang from the black stone.
Dust rose from his blow,
And those who saw it nearly died.
Choro began to show his strength,
And his many sworn enemies
Renounced not only their livestock
But even their lives entirely.
It was then that brave Seytek,
Questioning his uncle,
Entered the mountain fastness
And became embroiled in a great
And incurable tumult.
He entered a calamity that would not subside,
And became embroiled in a dispute.
“My precious uncle, bloodthirsty lion,
Sing and tell your song;
Tell your truth as solemnly as your creed.
Uncle, reveal your secret.
While your fortune was unharmed,
While your gray-wolf uncle lived,
You reached Afghanistan and raided it.
If your army did not strike it,
How could Jet-Kait have remained intact?
You went and shattered Afghanistan;
If you did not crush and pulverize it,
If you did not subdue it,
How could Bakünchö have remained intact?
While the hulking gray wolf lived,
You leveled men with your keen steel
And ruled every land you encountered.
We shattered them and took revenge.
We broke Altai and seized its valleys.
We routed the caravaners and took their tea.
While my lion-hearted uncle lived,
We hardened ourselves, sated with blood.
Throughout the world we were named “bloodthirsty.”
If told to take a cap, we cut off a head;
If told to drink water, we drank poison;
If told to spill blood, we spilled our fury.
We covered the valley’s waters with fat.
When together we struck the vengeful foe,
We laid even our own fathers low.
When we were driven into utter fury,
Khan Manas’s forty choros—
Not forty warriors, but forty companions,
Each of the forty had a different way,
All forty were famed champions who shattered the age.
Their horses grew fat and battle-ready;
Gathering around Manas,
They became renowned as the Forty.
When a lord thrust a spear, they flew like bullets;
When they attacked, they destroyed lives.
We slew the forty choros;
We did it because of what they themselves had done.
They spared no life, however one pleaded,
Those forty choros who attacked as one,
Whose knives were ever ready to slaughter.
Those forty choros went forth prepared,
And when they enraged us bitterly,
We destroyed the forty nobles
And made their women and girls weep.
From the forty courts of the forty choros,
We swept like wind and seized the ridge,
And wrought a mighty slaughter.
When they truly provoked our wrath,
We overthrew Abyke,
Sent Köbösh to the grave,
And showed every accursed enemy
The valor of gray wolves.
We anointed the white steel with blood.
Now tell the truth of your dire ordeals!
Tell of the saddlecloth you rode forth upon,
Tell of the valor that routed that host!”
When Seytek pressed him thus,
How could Choro remain silent?
If Külchoro refused to speak,
Could there ever be another like him?
“Fatherless brave Seytek, my son,
You would have me sing my song;
You would have me recount my scars.
You would have me begin the siege,
Hero, you would have me intensify the calamity.
You would hear my words,
Hero, you would have me vent my spirit!
You have brought this sorrow-laden head
To a halt at Kapka-Tash;
Why awaken the madness of long ago?
If I speak of my former days,
